advisor.summary: An aircraft used predominantly in a real trade or business supports very large deductions — operating costs under §162 and cost recovery including permanent 100 percent bonus — and attracts more concentrated IRS attention than anything else in this library. It is §280F listed property requiring more-than-50-percent qualified business use proven flight by flight; entertainment use disallows a proportionate share of every cost, depreciation included, under the occupied-seat rules; personal flights by owners impute income under the SIFL formula; and LB&I has run a dedicated business-aircraft audit campaign since February 2024. The engine deducts a single advisor-supplied figure taken from the separate depreciation and cost study — never present this strategy without that study underneath it, and build the file as if the exam notice were already in the mail.
mechanics: Deductibility starts with §162: recurring business transportation needs that commercial schedules serve poorly — multi-site operations, dispersed clients, time-critical work — documented flight by flight with route, passengers, and purpose.

Aircraft are listed property under §280F(d)(4): accelerated and bonus depreciation demand qualified business use above 50 percent in every year of the recovery period, and one failing year triggers recapture plus straight-line ADS from then on.

Entertainment use is carved out by Reg. §1.274-10: every cost, depreciation included, is allocated across occupied seats flight by flight, and the entertainment share is disallowed even when income is imputed to the executive.

Personal non-entertainment flights by owner-employees impute compensation under the SIFL rules of Reg. §1.61-21(g) — payroll has to run the numbers in practice, and the mismatch between deduction and imputed compensation is a standing exam adjustment.
Where profit motive is thin, §183 caps the activity's deductions; owner-to-business leasing structures add §469 self-rental and state sales-and-use issues that demand their own analysis.

The model applies one number — the annual business-use deduction from the separate study — as an entity deduction; depreciation schedules, entertainment disallowance, and SIFL all live in that study, not in the engine.

authority.note: The ordinary-and-necessary foundation — the business case behind every flight.
Listed-property status: the more-than-50-percent qualified-business-use test, with recapture and ADS on failure.
Permanent 100 percent bonus for qualifying aircraft acquired after January 19, 2025 — the figure that makes year one enormous.
Occupied-seat allocation disallowing the entertainment share of all aircraft costs, depreciation included.
The SIFL valuation formula for imputing owner-employees' personal flights as income.
Hobby-loss and passive/self-rental limits when the structure lacks a solid profit motive.
The LB&I business-aircraft audit campaign — why this file is built exam-first.

requirements: A genuine, recurring transportation need that commercial travel serves poorly — proven with routes and schedules, not adjectives.
Qualified business use above 50 percent, backed by contemporaneous flight-by-flight logs.
A standalone depreciation and operating-cost study that produces the annual deduction the model applies.
SIFL imputation running through payroll and the annual entertainment-use allocation computed.
FAA, insurance, and state sales-and-use coordination handled outside this model.
risks: Elevated audit probability is not hypothetical: the LB&I campaign announced in IR-2024-46 targets exactly this deduction, and its leading theory is personal and entertainment use dressed up as business — build the position assuming examination.
One personal-heavy flying season can gut the year: the occupied-seat allocation disallows a proportionate share of every cost, bonus depreciation included.
Business use at or below 50 percent in any recovery-period year triggers listed-property recapture and ADS from that point forward.
Missed SIFL imputation stacks payroll-tax exposure on top of the income-tax adjustment.
A weak profit motive invites §183 recharacterization, and the economics rarely pencil on tax savings alone — the aircraft must make business sense before tax.
stateNotes: Conformity: state depreciation decoupling bites hardest here — a bonus-decoupled state spreads the headline deduction over years, and state sales-and-use tax on the acquisition is often the largest non-federal number in the deal.
PTET interaction: the deduction reduces electing-entity income before any pass-through entity tax computation — a swing this large requires a PTET estimate reset.

Missouri: conforms to federal bonus through rolling conformity (RSMo §143.091); scope Missouri sales/use tax on the acquisition, and on any owner-to-entity lease, with the state filings before closing.
reviewChecklist: The separate aircraft study exists, is current, and supplies the exact number the model applies — no study, no strategy.
Flight logs reviewed: route, passengers, and per-seat purpose classification for every flight.
Business-use percentage above 50 percent with margin to spare, not at the line.
SIFL entries confirmed in payroll and the entertainment allocation reconciled.
Client sign-off in writing on the audit posture and the documentation burden.

client.teaser: A major deduction for a genuine business tool — with rules to match.
client.headline: When the plane is truly a business tool, the tax law treats it that way
plainEnglish: If your business truly depends on private air travel — several locations, clients spread across the map, schedules airlines cannot meet — the tax law allows real deductions. The operating costs of business flights count. So can a very large first-year write-off on the aircraft itself.

This is also one of the most closely watched deductions in the tax code. The IRS runs a special audit program for business aircraft. Every flight needs a log showing who was aboard and why. Personal trips get added to your income at set rates, and vacation-style flights cancel part of the deduction.

None of that is a reason to walk away. It is a reason to do it right. We make sure the numbers come from a real study, the records start with the first flight, and the deduction we claim is one we can defend without flinching.
